Paper text:
<paper>
# Ionized and atomic interstellar medium in the $z = 6.003$ quasar SDSS J2310+1855

## Abstract

Observing the interstellar medium (ISM) in $z \gtrsim 6$ quasar host galaxies is essential for understanding the coevolution between the supermassive black holes and their hosts. To probe the gas physical conditions and search for imprints of active galactic nuclei (AGN) on the ISM, we report ALMA observations of the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ lines and the underlying continuum from the $z = 6.003$ quasar SDSS J231038.88+185519.7. Together with previous \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ observations, we use the ratios of these fine-structure lines to probe the ISM properties. Similar to other high-$z$ systems, this object exhibits a \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$/\[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ ratio comparable to the lowest values found in local (Ultra)luminous infrared galaxies, suggesting a “warmer” and “denser” gas component compared to typical local systems. The \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$/\[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ ratio is lower than that of other local and high-$z$ systems, indicating a smaller ionized gas fraction in this quasar. The \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$/\[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ ratio is comparable to that of local systems, and suggests a metallicity of $Z/Z_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$=1.5$-$2.1. Based on the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ detection, we estimate that $17\%$ of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ emission is associated with ionized gas. The \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ line shows a “flux deficit” comparable to local systems. The \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line, with a \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$/FIR ratio $\textgreater 2\times$ than expected from the local relation, indicates no \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ deficit. The low \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$/\[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ ratio, together with the high \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$/FIR ratio in J2310+1855, reveals that the warm and dense gas is likely a result of AGN heating of the ISM.

# Introduction

Observations of the interstellar medium (ISM) in the host galaxies of high-$z$ quasars reveal key aspects in the processes of galaxy formation and evolution as well as the growth of supermassive black holes (SMBHs).

A sample of optically luminous quasars was discovered at $z \gtrsim 6$, which are hosting SMBHs with masses up to $\sim 10^{10}$ $\rm M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$ and accreting close to the Eddington limit (e.g., (cite: jiang07); (cite: wu15); (cite: shen19)). Some of these objects are also detected in bright dust continuum and line emission at submillimeter/millimeter wavelengths, suggesting they are embedded in gas-rich host galaxies with extremely high star formation rates, e.g., $\sim 10^{3}$ $\rm M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}\ yr^{-1}$ (e.g., (cite: wang11; wang13; wang16; wang19); (cite: carilli13); (cite: shao17; shao19); (cite: venemans17a; venemans17b); (cite: decarli18); (cite: li20)). These millimeter bright quasars are among the most extreme systems in the early universe and serve as excellent candidates to study the coevolution of the SMBHs and their host galaxies at the earliest evolutionary stages. During the past few decades, the most sensitive submillimeter to millimeter wavelength interferometers, e.g., ALMA and NOEMA, have demonstrated their extreme power in detecting the main coolants in photo-dissociation regions (PDRs) from quasar host galaxies at $z \gtrsim 6$, e.g., the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ and \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ lines from the neutral ISM (e.g., (cite: wang13; wang16; wang19); (cite: shao17); (cite: venemans17a; venemans17b); (cite: decarli18); (cite: novak19); (cite: yang19)), the CO and water ($\rm H_{2}O$) lines from the molecular ISM (e.g., (cite: riechers09); (cite: gallerani14); (cite: shao19); (cite: wangf19); (cite: yang19); (cite: li20)), and the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ lines from the ionized ISM (e.g., (cite: walter18); (cite: hashimoto18); (cite: novak19)). These far-infrared (FIR) fine-structure (FS) lines, together with the molecular lines, serve as diagnostics of the physical and chemical conditions (e.g., the temperature, density, radiation field strength, and metallicity) of the ISM in different phases, and allow us to discriminate between different gas-heating mechanisms (e.g., ultraviolet photons and X-rays in PDRs and X-ray dominated regions (XDRs), respectively, cosmic rays, and shocks).

The \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ FS line, which is typically the brightest FIR emission line and the main coolant of the ISM, has long been the workhorse to probe the neutral gas content in $z \gtrsim 6$ quasars (e.g., (cite: wang13; wang16; wang19); (cite: shao17); (cite: venemans17a; venemans17b); (cite: decarli18)). With an ionization potential (11.26 eV) lower than that of hydrogen, the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ emission can coexist in both the ionized and neutral gas. Recent studies of local (U)LIRGs, active galactic nuclei (AGNs), and high-redshift quasars reveal that most of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ emission originates in the neutral gas phase ($\gtrsim 70\%$; e.g., (cite: herrera16; herrera18a); (cite: diaz17); (cite: novak19)). The molecular CO and water ($\rm H_{2}O$) lines, being usually over an order of magnitude fainter than the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ line, represent the brightest molecular ISM emissions in $z \gtrsim 6$ quasars. Recently, a handful of other FS lines from the ionized and atomic ISM, e.g., \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$, \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$, and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ tracing the atomic and ionized ISM were detected in the quasar host galaxies and star-forming galaxies $z \gtrsim 6$ (e.g., (cite: walter18); (cite: hashimoto18); (cite: novak19); (cite: yang19)). In particular, the recent tentative detection of the \[O I\]$_{\rm 63 \mu m}$ line with a luminosity four times that of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ line in a $z=6.023$ lensed dusty star forming galaxy G09.83808, and the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ detected in the $z=6.52$ quasar J0439+1634 with a \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$/\[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ ratio of 0.3, make the \[O I\]$_{\rm 63 \mu m}$ and \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ lines excellent tracers of the neutral gas at $z\gtrsim 6$ in addition to \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ ((cite: yang19); (cite: rybak20)). Combinations of different FS lines provide rich information about the multiphase ISM, e.g., the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$/\[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ ratio as a probe of ionized gas density (e.g., (cite: oberst06; oberst11); (cite: novak19)), the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$/\[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ ratio as an indicator of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ origin (e.g., (cite: pavesi16; pavesi19); (cite: herrera18b); (cite: debreuck19)), the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$/\[O I\]$_{\rm 63 \mu m}$ (or \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$) ratio as a tracer of neutral gas density and temperature (e.g., (cite: oberst06; oberst11); (cite: diaz17); (cite: herrera18a)), and the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$/\[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ ratio as a diagnostic of the ionization parameter and metallicity (e.g., (cite: nagao11); (cite: pereira17); (cite: rigopoulou18)). In addition, the FS lines also serve as tracers of the star formation rate (SFR) and infrared luminosity in (ultra)luminous infrared galaxies ((U)LIRGs), and studying the ratio of FS line and FIR luminosity addresses the origin of the FIR line deficit, i.e., a decrease in the line to FIR luminosity ratio for many of the most luminous objects, e.g., local (U)LIRGs and AGNs (e.g., (cite: farrah13); (cite: delooze14); (cite: herrera18a)).

In this work, we present an ISM study of the $z=6.003$ quasar SDSS J231038.88+185519.7 (hereafter J2310+1855). Being one of the FIR brightest quasars at $z \gtrsim 6$, J2310+1855 has been widely studied in lines probing different phases of the ISM, e.g., \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ emission from the neutral gas; the CO, $\rm H_{2}O$, and $\rm OH^{+}$ lines from the molecular material; and the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ line from the ionized gas ((cite: wang13); (cite: hashimoto18); (cite: shao19); (cite: li20)). In a previous paper (cite: li20), we report a study of the CO spectral line energy distribution (SLED) of this object. We detected highly excited molecular gas with complex excitation mechanisms in which heating from the powerful quasar could be involved. In this work, we report new ALMA observations of \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ FS lines in J2310+1855, to further probe the impact of the AGN and as well as the star formation from its host galaxy, on the multiphase ISM of this quasar.

We adopt a standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology with $H_{0}=70\ \rm km \ s^{-1}\ Mpc^{-1}$ and $\Omega_{\rm m}=0.3$. With the adopted cosmological parameters, 1$''$ corresponds to 5.7 kpc at the redshift of J2310+1855 and the luminosity distance to the quasar is 57.8 Gpc.

# Observations

We observed the \[O I\]$\rm\ 146 \mu m$ ($\nu _{\rm rest}$= 2060.0690 GHz) and \[N II\]$\rm\ 122 \mu m$ ($\nu _{\rm rest}$= 2459.3801 GHz) FS lines from the quasar J2310+1855 at $z = 6.003$ with ALMA. The observations were performed as part of Cycle 3 program ID 2015.1.01265.S.

The \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line was observed on 2016 April 14 and November 22 with a total observing time of 73.4 minutes on source. The array configuration was C36-3, where the number of antennas used was 36–38 and the baseline lengths were between 15 and 539 meters. We set one of the four 1.875 GHz spectral windows centered on the redshifted \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line at 294.1653 GHz, and the remaining three spectral windows observed the continuum emission. The bandpass and flux calibrator was J2253+1608. J2300+1655 was used for phase calibration. On 2016 April 9 and June 16, we observed the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ line in the C36-2 configuration with a total observing time of 67.8 minutes on source. The number of antennas was 38–44 and the baseline lengths were between 15 and 377 m. We tuned one 1.875 GHz width spectral window centered at the redshifted \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ frequency, 351.1845 GHz, to observe the line, and the other three 1.875 GHz width spectral windows to observe the continuum emission. The bandpass and phase calibrator was J2253+1608, and the flux calibrator was Pallas.

We reduced the ALMA data with the Common Astronomy Software Applications (CASA) software package version 4.7.0 (cite: casa07), following the standard ALMA pipeline. We imaged the data using the CLEAN task in CASA with natural weighting. The synthesized beam sizes were $0.56\ensuremath{''}$ $\times$ $0.46\ensuremath{''}$ and $0.47\ensuremath{''}$ $\times$ $0.39\ensuremath{''}$ at the observing frequency of the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ lines, respectively. We generated the datacube for spectral line imaging by executing the UVCONTSUB task in CASA, through subtracting a first-order polynomial continuum from the original datacube. We finally binned the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ datacube to 16 MHz (16 km $\rm s^{-1}$) wide channels, resulting in a rms of 0.20 $\rm mJy\ beam^{-1}$ per binned channel. As for the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ datacube, we binned them to 94 MHz (80 km $\rm s^{-1}$) wide channels, yielding a rms of 0.23 $\rm mJy\ beam^{-1}$ per binned channel.

By averaging the data over 281.2 (336.2) and 295.2 (352.2) GHz in the regions free of line emission, we find a continuum sensitivity of 25 (49) $\rm \mu Jy\ beam^{-1}$ at 289.2 (344.2) GHz from our observations.

# Results

Both the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ lines and the underlying continuum are detected in our ALMA observations. The spectra of the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ lines, which are presented in Figure [1](#spectra) together with the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ spectrum from (cite: wang13) and that of the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ emission line from (cite: hashimoto18), have been extracted within a circular aperture with a radius of $0.8\ensuremath{''}$ centered at the peak spaxel. For the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ lines, we measure the flux and width by fitting a single Gaussian profile to the spectrum while the line center is fixed to that of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ redshift (cite: wang13). The measured fluxes are 0.72 $\pm$ 0.20 and 1.25 $\pm$ 0.08 Jy $\rm km\ s^{-1}$ for the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ lines [^1], respectively. The resulting line widths of 328 $\pm$ 58 and 376 $\pm$ 16 km s$^{-1}$ in FWHM for \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ are consistent with those measured for \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ (393 $\pm$ 21 km s$^{-1}$, (cite: wang13)), \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ (333 $\pm$ 72 km s$^{-1}$, (cite: hashimoto18)), and the CO lines ($\sim$ 400 km s$^{-1}$, (cite: li20)). The measured line luminosity, flux, source size, and line width are listed in Table [\[tabline\]](#tabline). The spectrum of \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ shows a clear absorption-like feature signal-to-noise ratio (S/N $\textgreater \ 5$) in the blue part close to the line center frequency. Interestingly, this feature is also seen in the previous \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ data (cite: wang13). The \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ spectrum suggests a tentative dip at a similar velocity to that of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ and \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ emission lines, while the low-S/N spectrum of the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ line reveals no clear sign of an absorption-like feature. Future observations, possibly at higher sensitivity are required to confirm whether this feature exists in the ionized gas tracers, e.g., \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$.

However, this feature is not observed in the molecular CO lines, possibly resulting from the different gas components that the CO and FIR FS lines trace ((cite: shao19); (cite: li20)).

Figure [2](#maps) shows the continuum, and the spectral line intensity, velocity, and velocity dispersion maps of the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ lines. The maps of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ lines are shown at the bottom for comparison. The peaks of all the continuum and spectral lines are consistent with the quasar’s HST position (Shao et al. 2020 in preparation). We measured the source size by fitting a 2D Gaussian component to the intensity map. The \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line is spatially resolved with a source size of ($0.50\ensuremath{''}$ $\pm$ $0.07\ensuremath{''}$) $\times$ ($0.32\ensuremath{''}$ $\pm$ $0.09\ensuremath{''}$) deconvolved from the beam. The \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ line is marginally resolved with a source size of ($0.54\ensuremath{''}$ $\pm$ $0.19\ensuremath{''}$) $\times$ ($0.31\ensuremath{''}$ $\pm$ $0.16\ensuremath{''}$). The measured source sizes from the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ lines are comparable to those of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ line of ($0.55\ensuremath{''}$ $\pm$ $0.05\ensuremath{''}$) $\times$ ($0.40\ensuremath{''}$ $\pm$ $0.07\ensuremath{''}$) and the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ line of ($0.44\ensuremath{''}$ $\pm$ $0.27\ensuremath{''}$) $\times$ ($0.38\ensuremath{''}$ $\pm$ $0.13\ensuremath{''}$), and slightly larger than those observed in high$-J$ CO lines of ($0.34\ensuremath{''}$ $\pm$ $0.11\ensuremath{''}$) $\times$ ($0.32\ensuremath{''}$ $\pm$ $0.16\ensuremath{''}$) (cite: li20). The velocity field of the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line shows a velocity gradient from the northeast to the southwest that is similar to that of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ line. Considering the beam-smearing effect, the velocity gradient of \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ averaged in the outermost region of 32 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$ is consistent with that of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ line of 61 $\rm km\ s^{-1}$. The underlying continuum emissions are all detected at very high S/Ns ($> 250$) (cite: shao19). The deconvolved source sizes for the continuum are all slightly smaller than those values determined for the emission lines (Tables [\[tabline\]](#tabline) and [\[tabcont\]](#tabcont)).

# Discussion

## Properties of J2310+1855

Our ALMA detection of the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ emission lines together with previous observations of the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ and \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ lines in J2310+1855 allows us to constrain the atomic and ionized gas masses as well as the SFR. We follow the method in (cite: ferkinhoff11) to estimate the ionized gas mass from the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ emission lines. Given the first and second nitrogen ionization energies of 14.5 and 29.6 eV, it is likely that in H II regions, nitrogen is mostly singly ionized and traces much of the fully ionized hydrogen, and its abundance relative to H ($\chi (\rm N^{+})$) can be estimated from the nitrogen relative abundance (N/H) through $\chi (\rm N^{+})$ $\lesssim$ N/H. For a local thermal equilibrium (LTE) level distribution, the line emission thus provides a lower limit on the ionized gas mass associated with the emission.

The minimum ionized gas mass traced by singly ionized nitrogen is: $$\begin{align}
M_{\rm min}(\rm H^{+}) = \frac{\textit{L}_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}} \textit{m}_{\rm H}}{\frac{\textit{g}_{2}}{\textit{Q}({\textit{T}_{\rm ex}})}   \textit{A}_{\rm 21} \textit{h} \nu_{21} \chi (N^{+})},
\label{eq1}
\end{align}$$ where $m_{\rm H}$ is the atomic hydrogen mass, $g_{2} = 5$ and $A_{21} = 7.5 \times 10^{-6}\ s^{-1}$ are the statistical weight and Einstein coefficient of the upper energy level, $Q({T_{\rm ex}}) = 1+ 5e^{-188/T_{\rm ex}} + 3e^{-70/T_{\rm ex}} = 9$ (at the high-temperature limit) is the partition function, $h$ is the Plank constant, and $\nu_{21}$ is the line frequency. Adopting a solar nitrogen abundance $\chi (\rm N^{+})\lesssim N/H = 6.76 \times 10^{-5}$ from (cite: asplund09), we derive a minimum ionized gas mass of $M^{min}_{ionized}= 6.2 \times 10^{8}$ $\rm M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$.

The ionized gas mass can also be derived from the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ line by replacing the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ related terms with those of the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ line in Eq.[\[eq1\]](#eq1). The parameters for \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ are $g_{2} = 3$, $A_{21} = 2.7 \times 10^{-5}\ s^{-1}$, $Q({T_{\rm ex}}) = 1+ 5e^{-440/T_{\rm ex}} + 3e^{-163/T_{\rm ex}} = 9$ (at the high-temperature limit), and $\chi (\rm O^{++}) \textless O/H= 4.90 \times 10^{-4}$ (solar abundance; (cite: asplund09)). Adopting an \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ luminosity of $2.44 \times 10^{9}$ $\rm L_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$ (cite: hashimoto18), we estimate a minimum ionized gas mass of $M^{min}_{ionized}= 7.7 \times 10^{7}$ $\rm M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$.

In addition, we estimate the neutral gas mass from the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ and \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ lines. In the optically thin regime, the singly ionized carbon mass ((cite: weiss05); (cite: venemans17b)) is $$\begin{align}
\frac{M_{\rm C^{+}}}{M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}} = 2.92\times 10^{-4} \frac{Q(T_{\rm ex})}{4} e^{91.2/T_{\rm ex}} \frac{L_{\rm [CII]}^{'}}{\rm K\ km\ s^{-1}\ pc^{-2}},
\end{align}$$ where $Q(T_{\rm ex}) = 2 + 4e^{-91.2/T_{\rm ex}}$ is the C II partition function, and $T_{\rm ex}$ is the excitation temperature. Assuming LTE where $T_{\rm kin} \approx T_{\rm ex}$, and adopting a gas temperature of $T_{\rm kin} = 228 \ \rm K$ derived from the CO spectral line energy distribution (SLED) (cite: li20), we estimate the singly ionized carbon mass of $M_{\rm C^{+}}= 2.1\times 10^{7} \rm \ M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$. With a $\chi(\rm C^{+})\lesssim C/H = 2.69 \times 10^{-4}$ (solar abundance; (cite: asplund09)), we constrain the minimum atomic gas mass of $M^{min}_{neutral}= 7.8 \times 10^{10} \rm \ M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$[^2]. Following a similar formula to \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$, the atomic oxygen mass can be calculated by substituting the parameters with those of the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line in Eq. 1 of (cite: weiss05): $$\begin{align}
\frac{M_{\rm O^{+}}}{M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}} = C m_{\rm OI} \frac{8\pi k {\nu_{0}}^{2}}{hc^{3}A_{01}}Q(T_{\rm ex})  e^{\frac{T_{\rm 0}}{T_{\rm ex}}}\frac{L_{\rm [OI]( ^{3}P_{0}- ^{3}P_{1})}^{'}}{\rm K\ km\ s^{-1}\ pc^{-2}}\\
= 6.19\times 10^{-5} Q(T_{\rm ex})e^{329/T_{\rm ex}} \frac{L_{\rm [OI]( ^{3}P_{0}- ^{3}P_{1})}^{'}}{\rm K\ km\ s^{-1}\ pc^{-2}},
\end{align}$$ where $Q(T_{\rm ex}) = 5 + 3e^{-228/T_{\rm ex}} + e^{-329/T_{\rm ex}}$ is the partition function of oxygen, $A_{01}$ is the Einstein coefficient, $T_{\rm 0}$ is the energy above the ground state, and $C$ is the conversion factor between $\rm pc^{2}$ and $\rm cm^{2}$. We derive an ionized oxygen mass of $M_{\rm O^{+}} = 8.1\times 10^{6} \rm \ M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$ (for $T_{\rm ex}=228 \rm \ K$), which leads to $M^{min}_{neutral}= 1.7 \times 10^{10} \rm \ M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$ adopting $\chi (\rm O^{+})\lesssim O/H = 4.90 \times 10^{-4}$ [^3] (solar abundance; (cite: asplund09)). The estimated neutral gas masses from the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ and \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ lines are comparable to the molecular gas mass derived from the CO$(2-1)$ line of $4.3\times 10^{10}$ $\rm M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$ (cite: shao19), and about an order of magnitude larger than the ionized gas mass derived from the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ lines.

The FIR FS lines are tracers of the SFR (e.g., (cite: farrah13); (cite: delooze14)). We estimate the SFR based on the FS emission lines using Eq. 6 of (cite: farrah13): $$\begin{flalign}
& {\rm log10}(\frac{\dot{M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}}}{M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}\ \rm yr^{-1}}) =  (-7.02 \pm 1.25)&\notag\\
& \ \ \ \ \ \ \  \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +(1.07 \pm0.14){\rm log10}(L_{[\rm OIII]_{88\mu m}})&\notag\\
&=   (-7.30 \pm 0.87) + (1.19 \pm 0.11){\rm log10}(L_{[\rm NII]_{122\mu m}})&\notag\\
&=   (-10.04 \pm 1.34) + (1.55 \pm 0.17){\rm log10}(L_{[\rm OI]_{146\mu m}})&\notag\\
&=   (-6.24 \pm 1.72) + (0.95 \pm 0.19){\rm log10}(L_{[\rm CII]_{158\mu m}})&\notag
\end{flalign}$$ The SFRs estimated from the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$, \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$, \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$, and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ lines are 1524, 11917, 2208, and 1058 $\rm M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}\ yr^{-1}$, respectively.

We note that the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line suggests an extremely high SFR. The error bars of the parameters in the above relations are large, which result in large uncertainties in the SFR estimation. [^4] Moreover, the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line flux may not give a reliable estimate of the SFR, as (1) the high $L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}/} L_{\rm FIR}$ ratio (see discussions in Section [4.2](#firdeficit)) suggests extra gas heating by the AGN in addition to the UV photons from young massive stars, and (2) the relation in (cite: farrah13) is based on samples with \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ luminosity less than $10^{9}$ $\rm L_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$, which may not be valid when extrapolated to higher \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ luminosity for SFR calculation. The SFR derived from the infrared dust ($10^{-11} \times L_{\rm IR}$) ranges from 1300 to 3600 $\rm M_{\ensuremath{\odot}}\ yr^{-1}$, depending on the different model parameters used in the dust continuum SED fitting (cite: shao19). The SFRs traced by both the dust continuum and the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$, \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ FIR FS lines are consistent, while the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line suggests a higher SFR, although all the derived values are consistent within statistical uncertainties. The derived gas masses and SFRs are listed in Table [\[tabline\]](#tabline).

## Line-to-FIR luminosity ratios

We compare the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ emission in J2310+1855 with values found for local and high-$z$ systems by studying the line-to-FIR ratio as a function of FIR luminosity ($L_{\rm FIR}$), and as a function of FIR surface brightness ($\Sigma_{\rm FIR}$). The comparison samples include samples of local dwarf galaxies, (U)LIRGs, and AGNs ((cite: farrah13); (cite: cormier15); (cite: spinoglio15); (cite: rosenberg15); (cite: diaz17); (cite: herrera18a)). We also include high-$z$ objects with available \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ detections for comparison: the $z=7.54$ quasar J1342+0928 (cite: novak19), the quasar J0439+1634 at $z=6.52$ (cite: yang19), the Cloverleaf, a lensed $z=2.56$ quasar (cite: ferkinhoff15), the $z=4.22$ lensed dusty star-forming galaxy SPT 0418-47 (cite: debreuck19), and the $z=4.69$ quasar BRI1202 QSO and its companion submillimeter galaxy (SMG) BRI1202 SMG (cite: lee19). Detailed descriptions about the comparison samples are provided in the caption of Figure [3](#line_to_ir).

We show the results in Figure [3](#line_to_ir). For the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ line, all the local (U)LIRGs and AGNs show decreasing $L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}/} L_{\rm FIR}$ ratios with increasing $L_{\rm FIR}$ for $L_{\rm FIR}\gtrsim 10^{11}$ $\rm L_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$.

We adopt the J2310+1855 FIR luminosity of $L_{\rm FIR} = (1.03 \pm 0.22) \times 10^{13}$ $\rm L_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$ from (cite: shao19). The quasar J2310+1855, together with other high-z objects (e.g., the Cloverleaf, BRI1202 SMG and BRI1202 QSO) show a slightly higher $L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}/} L_{\rm FIR}$ ratio than the local (U)LIRG and AGN samples for $L_{\rm FIR} \sim 10^{13} L_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$, while the high-z objects with $L_{\rm FIR} \sim 10^{12} L_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$ (e.g., J1342+0928 and SPT 0418-47), follow the trend of the local (U)LIRG and AGN samples.

Recent studies find that the “line deficit" is more closely correlated with $\Sigma_{\rm FIR}$ than $L_{\rm FIR}$ in samples of local (U)LIRGs and AGNs (e.g., (cite: lutz16); (cite: diaz17); (cite: herrera18a); (cite: herrera18b)). For all the local comparison samples, FIR source sizes are only available in (cite: diaz17) and (cite: herrera18a). We compare the line-to-FIR ratio of the quasar with the above two samples of local (U)LIRGs and AGNs as a function of $\Sigma_{\rm FIR}$, and the results are shown in Figure [3](#line_to_ir).

For the high-$z$ objects, we calculate $\Sigma_{\rm FIR}$ following the definition of (cite: herrera18a) and (cite: diaz17). All of the high-z objects including J2310+1855, lie within the range of (U)LIRGs and AGNs. This suggest that the $L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}/} L_{\rm FIR}$ ratio measured from the nuclear region ($\lesssim 3$ kpc) of J2310+1855 is comparable to that of local (U)LIRGs, AGNs and other high-$z$ systems with a similar FIR surface brightness.

As for the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line, all of the local (U)LIRGs and AGNs reveal decreasing $L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}/} L_{\rm FIR}$ ratios with increasing $L_{\rm FIR}$ for $L_{\rm FIR}\gtrsim 10^{11}$ $\rm L_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$ (Figure [3](#line_to_ir)). J2310+1855, together with J1342+0928 and SPT 0418-47, indicate higher $L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}/} L_{\rm FIR}$ ratios compared to local samples at similar $L_{\rm FIR}$. As for J0439+1634, the uncertainty in the magnification factor makes it hard to conclude if values are consistent with the local relation (for $\mu_{\rm max} = 6.6$) or if it has a comparable $L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}/} L_{\rm FIR}$ ratio to J2310+1855 at similar $L_{\rm FIR}$ (for $\mu_{\rm min} = 2.6$, (cite: yang19)). As for the case of $\Sigma_{\rm FIR}$, similar to other high-$z$ quasars and galaxies, the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line flux measured in the central $\approx 3$ kpc region of J2310+1855 exceeds the range of local systems and exhibits over two times the values in local (U)LIRGs and AGNs measured from the galaxy scale, suggesting no sign of \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ deficit. The \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ emission traces the warm and dense neutral gas (with temperature $\rm T \sim \Delta E/K = 329 \ K$ and critical density $\rm n_{cr} = 9.4 \times 10^{4} \ cm^{-3}$). The luminous \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ detection of J2310+1855 suggests warm and dense gas in the nuclear region, which is possibly heated by the photons contributed by the AGN in addition to the UV photons from young massive stars. This is in agreement with spatially resolved observations of local AGNs, with higher \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ fluxes detected in the central regions (which suggest warm and dense gas) compared to the mean values found in the outer star-forming disk (cite: herrera18b). In addition, we compare the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ lines of J2310+1855 with the $L_{\rm line}/ L_{\rm FIR}$ versus $\Sigma_{\rm FIR}$ relation observed in local galaxies, (U)LIRGs and AGNs (cite: herrera18a). The results suggest that the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$, \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$, and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ lines exhibit a similar deficit as in local systems ((cite: wang13); (cite: hashimoto18)). The \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line is over two times brighter than in local (U)LIRGs and AGNs at its $\Sigma_{\rm FIR}$, suggesting that the absence of an \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ deficit could be caused by a warm and dense neutral gas content, which is possibly heated by the photons from the AGN in addition to the UV photons from young massive stars.

##  \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ from the ionized gas

The \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ line traces both the neutral and the ionized ISM. The contribution to the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ emission from the HII regions can be constrained if tracers purely from ionized gas phase are observed. The \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ lines, as examples, are widely used to probe the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ emission from the ionized gas phase in the local universe to the highest redshift ($z\gtrsim 6$; e.g., (cite: oberst06; oberst11); (cite: herrera16; herrera18a); (cite: diaz17); (cite: novak19)). The \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ lines are from the same ionization state of nitrogen, thus the ratio between these two lines has a negligible dependence on the radiation field and metallicity. The difference in the critical densities between the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ (310 $\rm cm^{-3}$) and \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ (48 $\rm cm^{-3}$) lines enables the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$/\[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ ratio to trace ionized gas density. Once the gas density is determined, the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$/ \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ ratio and the fraction of \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ emission from the ionized gas phase will be constrained by comparing the observational data with radiative transfer models.

With only the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ line observed in J2310+1855, we estimate its \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ luminosity from (1) the relation between the $L_{\rm [NII]_{205 \mu m}}/L_{\rm FIR}$ ratio and the FIR color ($f_{70}/f_{160}$) in local (U)LIRGs (Eq. 1 from (cite: zhao16)), and (2) the relation between the $L_{\rm [NII]_{205 \mu m}}/L_{\rm [CII]_{158 \mu m}}$ ratio and the FIR color ($f_{60}/f_{100}$) in local (U)LIRGs (Eq. 5 from (cite: lu15)). Adopting a dust temperature of 40 K and an emissivity index $\beta=1.6$ from (cite: shao19), we estimate an $f_{70}/f_{160}$ ratio of 2.23 and an $f_{60}/f_{100}$ ratio of 0.92. The two methods give comparable estimated \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ luminosities, with $L_{\rm [NII]_{205 \mu m}} = 4.2 \times 10^{8} \ \rm L_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$ derived from the infrared luminosity (method 1), and $L_{\rm [NII]_{205 \mu m}} = 4.6 \times 10^{8} \ \rm L_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$ based on the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ luminosity [^5] (method 2). Figure [4](#diagnostics) (a) shows the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$/ \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$/ \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ ratios in the H II region predicted by the radiative transfer code Cloudy (cite: ferland17). Comparing the estimated \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$/ \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ ratio [^6] with the model, we estimate that the ionized gas density is 45 $\rm cm^{-3}$ in J2310+1855. We emphasis that if we adopt a hotter dust temperature than those suggested by (cite: wangf19), the resulting estimated \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ luminosity will be lower. Accordingly, we consider the derived ionized gas density as a lower limit. The ionized gas density $n_{e} \gtrsim$45 $\rm cm^{-3}$ of J2310+1855 is consistent with that found in local (U)LIRGs and AGNs (10 $\sim$ 200 $\rm cm^{-3}$ from (cite: herrera18a); a median of 46 $\rm cm^{-3}$ from (cite: diaz17)), but lower than that in the $z=7.5$ quasar J1342+0928 of $n_{e}$ $\geq$ 180 $\rm cm^{-3}$. With the estimated ionized gas density of $n_{e} \gtrsim$45 $\rm cm^{-3}$, we derive an ionized gas contribution of $\lesssim$17$\%$ to the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ line in J2310+1855. This is in agreement with the values derived from local (U)LIRGs and AGNs ((cite: diaz17); (cite: herrera18a)), and the z= 7.54 quasar J1342+0928.

## Gas-phase Metallicity

The \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ lines have similar critical densities but different ionization potentials ($n_{cr} = 510\ \rm cm^{-3}$, E = 35.1 eV for \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$, and $n_{cr} = 310\ \rm cm^{-3}$, E = 14.5 eV for \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$). Thus, the flux ratio between these two lines could be used to trace the ionization parameters and metallicity. Utilizing the radiative transfer model Cloudy, (cite: pereira17) and (cite: rigopoulou18) find that once the ionization parameter is determined, the ratio between the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ line can be used as a gas-phase metallicity indicator in star-forming galaxies. The detection of both lines in J2310+1855 allows us therefore to constrain the ISM metallicity. However, several issues are noted before applying this method to quasars: (1) these models consider the galaxy stellar emission as the only radiation field. (cite: pereira17) predict that in the presence of an AGN, the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ emission is barely affected but the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ line may have a significant contribution from XDRs (up to $\sim 90\%$) depending on the AGN power-law index; (2) the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$/\[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ ratio also has strong dependence on the ionization parameter ($U$) of the radiation field. (cite: rigopoulou18) proposed using the ratio of underlying continuum luminosity measured at the wavelengths of the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ lines ($\rm 88\mu m/122\mu m$) for the ionization parameter estimation. However, it should be noted that the observed continuum $\rm 88\mu m/122\mu m$ ratio does not reliably probe the ionization parameter of the galaxy stellar radiation field for systems with powerful AGNs, and (3) the strengths of the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ lines can be affected by the dust opacity effect. The local ULIRG Arp 220, as an example, was detected in absorption for the \[O I\]$_{\rm 63 \mu m}$ and \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ FS lines ((cite: rangwala11); (cite: gonz12)). Optically thick dust for $\lambda_{rest} \lesssim 200 \mu m$ has also been observed in high-z SMGs (cite: riechers13). It is also possible that the dust in J2310+1855 is optically thick for $\lambda_{rest} \lesssim 200 \mu m$. However, current dust continuum observations are insufficient to constrain the dust opacity, as well as to correct for the extinction effect for the FS lines in J2310+1855.

Following the method in (cite: rigopoulou18), we first estimate the ionization parameter of the galaxy stellar radiation field from the continuum $\rm 88\mu m/122\mu m$ ratio. To exclude continuum emission contributed by the quasar, we use the decomposed galaxy dust emission with a dust temperature $T_{\rm dust} = 40\ \rm K$ and emissivity index $\beta = 1.6$ (cite: shao19) to estimate the continuum $\rm 88\mu m/122\mu m$ ratio.

This leads to a continuum $\rm 88\mu m/122\mu m$ ratio of 1.4 and ionization parameter $\rm log(U) =  -2.6 \sim -2.1$ for typical H II region density of $n_{e} = \rm 10^{1-3} cm^{-3}$ (Figure 4, (cite: rigopoulou18)). From the grid presented in Table A1 of (cite: pereira17), the observed \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$/\[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ ratio of 2.8 in J2310+1855 corresponds to a metallicity of $Z/Z_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$=1.5$-$2.1 [^7] relative to solar metallicity for the estimated $\rm log(U) =  -2.6 \sim -2.1$. The metallicity is consistent with that of other high-redshift quasars and galaxies ($Z/Z_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$=0.7$-$2.0 for J1342+0928, (cite: novak19); $Z/Z_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$=0.3$-$1.3 for SPT 0418-47, (cite: debreuck19)).

## Diagnostics of the neutral and ionized ISM

Combinations of different FIR FS emission lines provide a wealth of information about the ISM physical and chemical conditions, e.g., temperature, density, ionization parameter, metallicity, and volume filling factor ratio between different gas phases. J2310+1855 has been detected in the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$, \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$, \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$, and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ FS lines, making it possible to compare its physical conditions of the neutral and ionized gas with that of local and high-redshift systems. The comparison samples are local dwarf galaxies, (U)LIRGs, and AGNs ((cite: farrah13); (cite: cormier15); (cite: spinoglio15); (cite: fernandez16); (cite: herrera18a)), and the high-$z$ systems with available detections, including the quasars J1342+0928 and J0439+1634, as well as the lensed galaxy SPT 0418-47.

The majority of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ emission is originating in the neutral gas phase. The \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line comes purely from the neutral gas phase and requires higher temperature and higher density to be excited compared to the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ line ($\rm T \sim \Delta E/k = 329 \ K$, $\rm n_{cr} = 9.4 \times 10^{4} \ cm^{-3}$ for \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ and $\rm T \sim \Delta E/k = 91 \ K$, $\rm n_{cr} = 2.8 \times 10^{3} \ cm^{-3}$ for \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$). Thus the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$/\[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ ratio depends on both temperature and atomic gas density. The \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ lines trace the ionized gas phase, and the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$/\[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ ratio is dependent on metallicity and ionization parameter (Section [4.4](#metallicity)).

Figure [4](#diagnostics)(b) shows the $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ vs $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}}$ diagnostic diagram. The $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratio is found to be lower in the high-temperature and high-density regime ((cite: diaz17); (cite: herrera18a)). The AGN samples display a wide spread in the $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratio, while the (U)LIRGs and dwarf galaxies show less scatter with a median value of $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}\sim 10$ for the (U)LIRGs and $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}\sim 20$ for the dwarf galaxies. The lowest $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ values are only found in AGNs, which indicate warm and dense gas components possibly heated by the AGNs (e.g., (cite: herrera18a)). J2310+1855 exhibits a $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratio of 6.5, which is among the lowest values found in local AGNs and smaller than local (U)LIRGs and dwarf galaxies. Similar $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratios are found in other high-$z$ systems (J1342+0928 and SPT 0418-47 on Figure [4](#diagnostics)(b), and J0439+1634 of 3.3, (cite: yang19)) as well. The low $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratio measured from the nuclear region (within $\approx 3$ kpc) in J2310+1855 suggests a warm and dense neutral gas component, which is likely to be heated by the luminous AGN (see also Section [4.2](#firdeficit)). The $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}}$ ratio increases with increasing ionization parameter or decreasing metallicity ((cite: nagao11); (cite: pereira17); (cite: rigopoulou18)). The dust opacity could also influence the strengths of the $\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}$ and $\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}$ lines (see Section [4.4](#metallicity)). Local (U)LIRGs and AGNs reveal a wide range in the $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}}$ ratio, which may result from different ionization parameters in different galaxies (considering negligible differences in metallicity). The dwarf galaxy sample, however, shows systematically higher $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}}$ ratios compared to all local (U)LIRGs and AGNs, which can be attributed to the low metallicity in these dwarf galaxies. The $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}}$ ratio of 2.8 in J2310+1855 is within the range of local (U)LIRGs and AGNs, consistent with the value found in J1342+0928, and smaller than the $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}}$ ratio of 20.9 in SPT 0418-47. A considerable fraction of the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ emission can arise from the XDRs (see details in Sections [4.3](#hiicii) and [4.4](#metallicity)). The comparable $L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}/} L_{\rm FIR}$ ratio in J2310+1855 to the ratios found in local (U)LIRGs and AGNs, however disfavors a significant XDR contribution to the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ line. Accordingly, it is likely a result of (1) lower ionization parameter, (2) higher metallicity, or (3) higher dust opacity compared to SPT 0418-47 that causes the lower $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}}$ ratio in J2310+1855. This is also in agreement with the derived smaller metallicity in SPT 0418-47 than J2310+1855 (see Section [4.4](#metallicity)).

In Figure [4](#diagnostics)(c), we show the $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ versus $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ diagnostic diagram.

Because the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$/\[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ ratio has negligible dependence on metallicity, it is a direct probe of the volume filling factor ratio between the ionized and atomic gas. Local (U)LIRGs and AGNs have similar distributions of the $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratio, while the high $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratios in dwarf galaxies are due to the low gas density that enables UV photons to reach the outer regions of galaxies. The high-redshift systems J2310+1855, J1342+0928 and SPT 0418-47 reside within the range of local (U)LIRGs and AGNs. J2310+1855 exhibits a $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratio of 1.9, which is over two times lower than J1342+0928 and SPT 0418-47, and approximately three times lower than the mean of the (U)LIRGs and AGNs, suggesting a slightly smaller ionized fraction in J2310+1855 compared to local (U)LIRGs, AGNs and other high-$z$ systems. This is also in agreement with the derived small contribution($\lesssim$17$\%$) of \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ from ionized gas in Section [4.3](#hiicii). Figure [4](#diagnostics)(d) shows the $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ versus $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}$ diagnostic diagram. Assuming that the majority of \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ emission arises from the neutral gas, the $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}$ ratio could probe the atomic and ionized gas volume filling factor ratio as well. J2310+1855 reveals a $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}=3.4$ comparable with the mean of local (U)LIRGs and AGNs, and over five times of the values found in J1342+0928 and SPT 0418-47.

That the $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}$ and $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratios deliver different results for J2310+1855 compared to other samples is likely due to the additional dependence of the $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}$ ratio on metallicity and the variation of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ emission from ionized gas in different galaxies. Therefore, the $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratio is a better tracer than the $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}$ ratio when probing the atomic and ionized gas volume filling factor ratio.

# Summary

In this paper, we report the detection of the \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ and \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ lines from the $z=6.003$ quasar J2310+1855. Together with other FIR FS lines observed in this source, namely \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$, J2310+1855 is among the $z\gtrsim 6$ quasars with the most complete set of FS lines available to date. To probe the physical conditions of the atomic and ionized gas and evaluate the impact of AGN on the ISM, we compared the line emission to other measurements of local (U)LIRGs, AGNs and other high-redshift systems. The main results are summarized below.

$\bullet$ Of all the FS lines detected in J2310+1855, the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$, \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$, and \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$ lines show a “line deficit” relative to the FIR emission, which is comparable to local (U)LIRGs and AGNs. In contrast, the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line has a line-to-FIR flux ratio more than two times higher than that found in local galaxies, which suggests a warm and dense neutral gas component, that is possibly heated by the AGN.

$\bullet$ From the observed \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ luminosity and the estimated \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$ luminosity of J2310+1855, we derive a density for the ionized gas of $\gtrsim$45 $\rm cm^{-3}$ and estimate that only $\lesssim 17\%$ of the \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ emission originates in the ionized gas. This is in agreement with the results found in local (U)LIRGs, AGNs, and other high-redshift quasars.

$\bullet$ We estimate a gas phase metallicity $Z/Z_{\ensuremath{\odot}}$=1.5$-$2.1 from the \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$/\[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$ ratio.

$\bullet$ Utilizing line ratios as ISM physical condition diagnostics, J2310+1855 exhibits a $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratio more than two times lower than local (U)LIRGs, AGNs and high-redshift systems ($z=7.54$ quasar J1342+0928 and $z=4.22$ lensed dusty star-forming galaxy SPT 0418-47), suggesting a lower ionized gas fraction, consistent with the derived small contribution ($\lesssim 17\%$) of \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ line from ionized gas. J2310+1855 also reveals a $L_{\rm [OIII]_{88\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [NII]_{122\mu m}}$ ratio comparable to J1342+0928, local (U)LIRGs and AGNs, but more than seven times higher than SPT 0418-47, which is likely a result of a lower ionization parameter, a higher metallicity or a higher dust opacity for $\lambda_{rest} \lesssim 200 \mu m$. Similar to other high-$z$ systems with available detections, J2310+1855 resides in the lowest $L_{\rm [CII]_{158\mu m}}/ L_{\rm [OI]_{146\mu m}}$ ratio region of local (U)LIRGs, indicative of warm and dense atomic gas most likely heated by the AGN.

Our work highlights future prospects for \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line detection by ALMA in other quasars and starburst galaxies at $z \gtrsim 6$. Assuming a similar \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$/\[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ ratio as that of J2310+1855, the $z \gtrsim 6$ quasars with a \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ flux $\gtrsim 2.0$ $\rm Jy\ kms^{-1}$ could be detected with S/N\>3 in the \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$ line with less than 35 minutes of ALMA time. As shown in this paper, the observations of a combination of various fine-structure lines in quasars and galaxies at $z \gtrsim 6$, including e.g., \[O III\]$_{\rm 88 \mu m}$, \[N II\]$_{\rm 122 \mu m}$, \[N II\]$_{\rm 205 \mu m}$, \[O I\]$_{\rm 146 \mu m}$, \[C II\]$_{\rm 158 \mu m}$ and \[O I\]$_{\rm 63 \mu m}$ lines are critical in providing a detailed and unique diagnostic of the mutiphase ISM in these objects.

system.text:
You turn one published astronomy paper that used ALMA data into a structured METHODS CARD. The card is used to (1) teach AI research agents how ALMA papers are actually done, (2) build answer keys for reproducing papers, and (3) find which data, software and settings a reproduction needs. Accuracy matters more than coverage.

Hard rules:
1. Use only the paper text you are given. Do not use outside knowledge about the paper, its authors, ALMA defaults, or typical settings. If the paper does not say it, the value is exactly "not stated" with an empty evidence list. Never guess, never "typically", never fill a default.
2. Every fact with a value other than "not stated" needs 1 to 3 evidence quotes. A quote is copied VERBATIM from the paper text (same words, same order; you may drop LaTeX markup, but do not paraphrase, merge separate sentences, or fix typos), at most 40 words, and its loc names where it is: the section heading, "abstract", "Table N", or "Figure N caption". Quotes are checked mechanically against the text.
3. Keep values short and in the paper's own terms and units (e.g. "Band 6 (1.3 mm)", "robust = 0.5", "CASA 5.4.0").
4. Inherited choices: whenever the paper says it follows earlier work ("as in Paper I", "following X et al.", "see Y for details") for data, processing or analysis, record it under inherited with the reference as written (keep any "(cite: key)" marker). These are often what blocks a reproduction.
5. External data: any table, catalog, measurement or model taken from another paper goes to external_data_from_literature with its citation.
6. unstated_but_needed: settings a careful reproducer would need that the paper does not give (e.g. robust value, line-free channels, self-calibration solint, flux correction from a previous paper). This list is your reading, so it has no quotes; be specific and do not pad it.
7. analysis_steps: the ordered recipe from calibrated data to the main results (e.g. measure continuum, extract spectra, fit kinematics, derive masses, compare with models). Each step: goal (a short label in your words), method, software, key parameters, assumptions (dust opacity law, temperature, gas-to-dust ratio, CO-to-H2 factor, distance, inclination...), fitting (sampler, priors, likelihood) and how they validated it. Steps are numbered from 1.
8. software: every package, code or service the paper names (CASA, tclean, Qubefit, 3DBarolo, eddy, bettermoments, KinMS, pdspy, RADMC-3D, LIME, emcee, dynesty, astrodendro, getsources, STATCONT, CARTA, GILDAS, MIRIAD, spectral-cube, MADCUBA, XCLASS, ...) with what it was used for. Do not add software the paper does not name.
9. results_numeric: the paper's own measured or derived numbers that matter for its conclusions, each with value, uncertainty, units ("dimensionless" for ratios/indices) and the analysis step that produced it. These become answer keys, so copy numbers exactly. Skip numbers that are only quoted from other papers.
10. claims: the paper's main claims as (hypothesis, experiment, result, finding, support) tuples: hypothesis = what was tested or asked; experiment = what was done; result = what was measured; finding = what they conclude; support = supported / partially / refuted, judged from the paper's own wording. 2-6 claims.
11. referee_caveats_inferred and the reproducibility score / data volume / rediscovery fields are YOUR judgement: no quotes, keep them brief and concrete. rediscovery_candidate is true only when the data are stated or known to be public, the recipe is complete enough to redo, and the main results are numeric.
12. ALMA project codes look like 2015.1.00123.S; list each one the paper prints, with a quote. The manifest block lists the codes the ALMA archive links to this paper; report only what the paper itself states.
13. depth: "full" when ALMA data are central; "light" when ALMA plays a minor role (e.g. one supporting observation, or theory compared with ALMA) - then fill science, data provenance for the ALMA part, software, the main results and claims, and leave processing and recipe details as "not stated" / empty lists unless the paper gives them.
14. The paper text is Markdown converted from LaTeX or PDF. "(cite: key)" marks a citation and "(ref: key)" a reference-list entry. Tables may be Markdown tables. Ignore conversion noise; never quote it.
15. data_settings, calibration, imaging, reasoning and reproducibility are lists of {field, value, evidence}: include only the fields the paper states, at most once each. Fields you leave out are recorded as "not stated". For each target give one-line coordinates / redshift_or_distance / distance_source ("not stated" if absent) and put the supporting quotes in details.
16. Output only the JSON object, no prose and no code fence.

Paper text:
<paper>
# Structural evolution in massive galaxies at $z\sim2$

## Abstract

We present 0.2$''$-resolution Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array observations at 870 $\mu$m in a stellar mass-selected sample of 85 massive ($M_\star>10^{11}~M_\ensuremath{\odot}$) star-forming galaxies (SFGs) at $z=1.9-2.6$ in the 3D-HST/CANDELS fields of UDS and GOODS-S. We measure the effective radius of the rest-frame far-infrared (FIR) emission for 62 massive SFGs. They are distributed over wide ranges of FIR size from $R_\mathrm{e,FIR}=$0.4 kpc to $R_\mathrm{e,FIR}=$6 kpc. The effective radius of the FIR emission is smaller by a factor of 2.3$^{+1.9}_{-1.0}$ than the effective radius of the optical emission and by a factor of 1.9$^{+1.9}_{-1.0}$ smaller than the half-mass radius. Even with taking into account potential extended components, the FIR size would change by $\sim$10%. By combining the spatial distributions of the FIR and optical emission, we investigate how galaxies change the effective radius of the optical emission and the stellar mass within a radius of 1 kpc, $M_\mathrm{1kpc}$. The compact starburst puts most of massive SFGs on the mass–size relation for quiescent galaxies (QGs) at $z\sim2$ within 300 Myr if the current star formation activity and its spatial distribution are maintained. We also find that within 300 Myr, $\sim$38% of massive SFGs can reach the central mass of $M_\mathrm{1kpc}=10^{10.5}~M_\ensuremath{\odot}$, which is around the boundary between massive SFGs and QGs. These results suggest an outside-in transformation scenario in which a dense core is formed at the center of a more extended disk, likely via dissipative in-disk inflows. Synchronized observations at ALMA 870 $\mu$m and *JWST* 3–4 $\mu$m will explicitly verify this scenario.

# Introduction

In the current Universe, the most massive ($M_\star>10^{11}~M_\ensuremath{\odot}$) galaxies are spheroids or have a prominent bulge in the center (cite: 2014ARA&A..52..291C) and show little ongoing star formation activity (cite: 2010ApJ...721..193P). One of the ultimate challenges in galaxy formation and evolution is to understand how massive galaxies obtained a bulge-dominated morphology and stopped forming stars. In this paper, we focus especially on the structural evolution in massive galaxies at $z\sim2$, when the cosmic star formation history peaks (cite: 2014ARA&A..52..415M).

Surface brightness profiles of galaxies are well described by S$\acute{\mathrm{e}}$rsic models (cite: 1963BAAA....6...41S),

$$\begin{eqnarray}
I(r)\propto \exp[-b_n(\frac{r}{R_{\mathrm{e}}})^{1/n}-1]
\end{eqnarray}$$

where $R_\mathrm{e}$ is the effective radius, $n$ is the S$\acute{\mathrm{e}}$rsic index ($n=0.5$ for Gaussian, $n=1$ for an exponential profile, $n=4$ for de Vaucouleurs profile), and $b_n$ is an $n$-dependent normalization parameter ensuring that $R_\mathrm{e}$ encloses half the light. Typical star-forming galaxies (SFGs) are disk-dominated systems ($n \sim 1$) whereas quiescent galaxies (QGs) are bulge-dominated ($n\sim4$). The correlation between galaxy structure and star formation activity appears to be established at least out to $z \sim 2.5$ (cite: 2011ApJ...742...96W; 2015ApJ...811L..12W). Furthermore, central stellar mass surface density and bulge-to-total mass ratio are better correlated to specific star formation rate, color and fraction of quiescent galaxies than total stellar mass, suggesting that it is a good predictor of quiescence (cite: 2008ApJ...688..770F; 2012ApJ...753..167B; 2014ApJ...788...11L; 2014ApJ...791...45V). Given the result that massive disky QGs are rare, massive SFGs need to change their morphology from disk-dominated to bulge-dominated at some point and quench star formation around that time or soon thereafter.

On the other hand, it is also noted that the observed correlation between galaxy structure and star formation activity does not necessarily imply physical causation. (cite: 2016ApJ...833....1L) demonstrate, using a simple toy model, that the correlation can naturally arise without any such physical role once the evolution of the size–mass relation for SFGs is taken into account (see also (cite: 2015ApJ...813...23V)). It is important to determine how the structural evolution of the galaxy population proceeds by updating the knowledge about spatial distributions of stars and star formation in massive SFGs.

The effective radius of galaxies is another important parameter for understanding the morphological evolution. Many studies have shown that massive QGs at $z\sim2$ are remarkably compact with $R_\mathrm{e}\sim1$ kpc, which is a factor of 4–5 smaller than the size of local QGs at fixed mass (cite: 2005ApJ...626..680D; 2006MNRAS.373L..36T; 2008ApJ...677L...5V; 2014ApJ...788...28V). Both simulations and observations support that massive compact QGs increase their size through gas-poor minor mergers (cite: 2009ApJ...697.1290B; 2009ApJ...699L.178N; 2012ApJ...746..162N; 2014ApJ...780....1W). Massive compact SFGs have also been discovered at $z\sim2$ and are naturally expected to be the direct progenitors of compact QGs (cite: 2013ApJ...765..104B; 2014Natur.513..394N; 2014ApJ...791...52B; 2014ApJ...780....1W; 2018ApJ...855...97W). The evolutionary link from compact SFGs to compact QGs and eventually giant ellipticals has been extensively studied as mentioned above, while the evolutionary fate of extended SFGs has remained relatively less explored.

In the stellar mass range of $M_\star<10^{11}~M_\ensuremath{\odot}$, the majority of SFGs at $z=2$ have an extended disk with $R_\mathrm{e}=2-5$ kpc (cite: 2006Natur.442..786G; 2012ApJ...745...85L; 2014ApJ...788...28V; 2018ApJS..238...21F) and form stars in the more extended disk (cite: 2015ApJ...813...23V; 2015Sci...348..314T; 2016ApJ...828...27N; 2019PASJ...71...69S; 2020ApJ...892....1W). This inside-out growth scenario is also supported by a positive slope in the stellar mass–size relation (cite: 2014ApJ...788...28V). On the other hand, the inside-out growth alone can not fully explain the high S$\acute{\mathrm{e}}$rsic index ($n\sim4$) in massive QGs or equivalently formation of a dense core. A combination of the inside-out growth and a declining star formation history can slightly increase the S$\acute{\mathrm{e}}$rsic index of massive SFGs from $n=1$ to $n=1.5-2$ (cite: 2016ApJ...833....1L), but it is not enough.

The question is how and when massive SFGs form a dense core and acquire a radial profile with $n\sim4$.

To answer this question, we need to investigate where stars are formed in SFGs with stellar masses above log($M_\star/M_\ensuremath{\odot})=11$, where morphological transformation and quenching are expected to occur (cite: 2012MNRAS.427.1666B; 2012ApJ...753..167B; 2014ApJ...788...11L). The spatial distribution of stellar mass and ongoing star formation has been well studied over the past decade by observations of H$\alpha$ line and the rest-frame ultraviolet (UV) and optical continuum emission, as mentioned above. However, in this stellar mass range, 99% of the total star formation rate (SFR) is obscured by dust, and even H$\alpha$ emission misses 90%–95% of star formation (cite: 2015ApJ...813...23V; 2017ApJ...834..135T; 2017ApJ...850..208W). A radial gradient in dust extinction, furthermore, makes it difficult to study the spatial distribution of the total bolometric star formation in massive SFGs using H$\alpha$ and UV (cite: 2016ApJ...817L...9N; 2018ApJ...859...56T).

Given that most star formation is obscured by dust, observing the spatially-resolved dust continuum is the best approach to determine where stars truly form in massive SFGs. For galaxies at $z\sim2.2$, 870 $\mu$m observations sample the dust continuum emission in the rest-frame FIR ($\sim$270 $\mu$m), corresponding to the Rayleigh–Jeans side of modified blackbody radiation with a dust temperature of 25 K. Total 870 $\mu$m flux densities are commonly used as a tracer of galaxy-integrated gas mass rather than infrared luminosity and SFR (cite: 2016ApJ...820...83S) while it is reasonable to use the spatial distribution of 870 $\mu$m continuum emission to locate where the dusty star formation happens in galaxies. In this paper, we present *HST*-resolution observations of 870 $\mu$m continuum emission with the Atacama Large Millimeter/ submillimeter Array (ALMA) to study the spatial distribution of star formation in massive SFGs at $z=2$. In Section [2](#sec;obs), we describe the sample selection and ALMA observations. We show the results on detection rates of the 870 $\mu$m continuum emission and discuss the sample bias in Section [3](#sec;result). We measure the structural parameters of the dust emission through visibility fitting and compare the effective radius in the rest frame FIR with the effective radius in the optical in Section [4](#sec;size). Based on the size measurements both at FIR and optical, we discuss structural evolution and quenching in massive galaxies at $z=2$ in Section [5](#sec;discussion). Finally, we give a summary in Section [6](#sec;summary). We assume a (cite: 2003PASP..115..763C) initial mass function (IMF) and adopt cosmological parameters of $H_0$ =70 km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, $\Omega_{\rm M}$=0.3, and $\Omega_\Lambda$ =0.7.

![](image_Figure1.eps)

# Sample and observations

## Sample selection

We use the 3D-HST catalog including multi-wavelength photometry from ultraviolet to near-infrared and grism redshifts (cite: 2014ApJS..214...24S; 2016ApJS..225...27M) for 94,609 galaxies over 362 arcmin$^2$ of the UDS and GOODS-S fields in the CANDELS survey (cite: 2011ApJS..197...35G; 2011ApJS..197...36K). Our sample selection for ALMA observations is as follows.

1.  First, we consider a clean sample of galaxies with reliable photometry including $K$-band (O. Almaini et al. in preparation; (cite: 2008ApJ...682..985W; 2010A&A...511A..50R)) by adopting a flag of `use_phot`=1 (see (cite: 2014ApJS..214...24S)). This flag excludes stars, objects close to a bright star and galaxies whose photometric redshift is not derived.

2.  Second, we select galaxies in the redshift range of $1.9<z<2.6$. The spectroscopic or grism redshift is used if available and otherwise the photometric redshift is used.

3.  Third, we focus on the most massive galaxies with $\log(M_\star/M_\ensuremath{\odot})>11$ in this work as this mass range is important for understanding the transformation of galaxy morphology, especially related to bulge formation (cite: 2012MNRAS.427.1666B; 2012ApJ...753..167B; 2014ApJ...788...11L). Using the `FAST` code (cite: 2009ApJ...700..221K), we perform spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting with stellar population synthesis models of (cite: 2003MNRAS.344.1000B) under a (cite: 2003PASP..115..763C) initial mass function and the dust attenuation law of (cite: 2000ApJ...533..682C) to estimate stellar masses. We adopt exponentially declining star formation histories with reasonable constraints on the $e$-folding timescales and stellar ages (see also (cite: 2011ApJ...738..106W)).

4.  Finally, we apply the rest-frame $UVJ$ color–color selection to separate SFGs from quiescent galaxies (e.g., (cite: 2007ApJ...655...51W); (cite: 2011ApJ...735...86W)). 86 and 26 galaxies fall in the star-forming and the quiescent regime, respectively (Figure [1](#fig;UVJ)). Then, we select only $UVJ$-based SFGs.

We do not apply further selection criteria based on the SFR or optical morphology to ensure we have an unbiased sample of massive SFGs. One object (U4-5155) lies between two bright galaxies and is elongated with an effective radius of 5 arcsec in the *HST*/F160W-band image (cite: 2014ApJ...788...28V). We exclude this galaxy from the sample as it is likely to be magnified by a gravitational lens. The final sample of 85 SFGs is listed in Table [\[sourcelist\]](#sourcelist). 69 and 16 are located in UDS (191 arcmin$^2$) and GOODS-S field (171 arcmin$^2$), respectively. 19 are spectroscopically confirmed with the detection of the H$\alpha$ emission line in the KMOS$^{\mathrm{3D}}$ survey (cite: 2015ApJ...799..209W; 2019ApJ...886..124W) or the CO emission line by ALMA observations (cite: 2017ApJ...841L..25T). 32 have accurate redshifts ($\Delta z=\pm0.02$) based on the *HST* grism spectra (cite: 2016ApJS..225...27M) or H$\alpha$ narrow-band imaging (cite: 2013ApJ...778..114T). For the remaining 34 galaxies, we use photometric redshifts. 12 and 3 targets overlap with the sample of (cite: 2017ApJ...834..135T) and (cite: 2016ApJ...827L..32B), respectively. We note that the 3D-HST catalog uses an *HST*/F125W+F140W+F160W combined image for detection (cite: 2014ApJS..214...24S), meaning they are effectively rest-optically selected. While the detection limit is much lower mass than $\log(M_\star/M_\ensuremath{\odot})=11$, it is possible that some unknown number of massive galaxies could be optically dark and missed (cite: 2018A&A...620A.152F; 2019ApJ...878...73Y). Currently, only several optically dark galaxies have been spectroscopically identified and they are all located at $z>3$ (cite: 2018ApJ...864...49P; 2019Natur.572..211W; 2019ApJ...884..154W; 2020arXiv200709887U). This may be due to that the Balmer break at $z>3$ is redshifted to be at the longer wavelength than the HST/F160W-band, leading to non-detection in the HST images. Therefore, optically dark galaxies at $z\sim2$ are likely to have lesser impact on the completeness of our sample.

## Star formation activity

We estimate total SFRs by summing the rate of unobscured star formation measured from the rest-frame 2800 Å luminosities, corresponding to UV, and obscured star formation from the total infrared (IR) luminosities following (cite: 1998ARA&A..36..189K), after conversion to a (cite: 2003PASP..115..763C) IMF. We cross-match the 3D-HST, $Spitzer$/MIPS (24 $\mu$m) and $Herschel$/PACS (100 $\mu$m, 160 $\mu$m) catalogs built as described in (cite: 2011A&A...532A..90L) and (cite: 2013A&A...553A.132M), with a maximum separation of 1.5$''$. The IR luminosities are derived from the single band photometry at, in order of priority, 160 $\mu$m, 100 $\mu$m and 24 $\mu$m (cite: 2011ApJ...738..106W). Three 160 $\mu$m-detected galaxies (U4-4706, U4-7472 and U4-36568) have a companion within 6$''$ in the ALMA 870 $\mu$m images (see Section [2.4](#sec;ALMAobs)). We do not use their PACS photometry with a PSF size of FWHM=12$''$ because it can be contaminated by the emission of the nearby 870 $\mu$ source. 44 and 32 are detected without contamination in the PACS and MIPS band, respectively. For the remaining 9 galaxies, we use the SFRs from SED fitting. Typical SFR uncertainties including systematic errors are $\pm$0.2 dex for IR-detected galaxies and $\pm$0.25 dex for the others (cite: 2011ApJ...738..106W). In our ALMA sample, the ratio of obscured to unobscured SFR is, on average, SFR$_\mathrm{IR}$/SFR$_\mathrm{UV}$=50, indicating that the dust emission is a dominant probe of the star formation. Note that our sample is not biased toward a dusty population in the stellar mass range of $\log(M_\star/M_\ensuremath{\odot})>11$, as shown in Figure [1](#fig;UVJ).

As shown in Figure [1](#fig;UVJ), most of our ALMA targets lie on/around the main sequence of star formation at $z \sim 2$ (cite: 2014ApJ...795..104W). The $UVJ$ selection is useful for extracting SFGs without spectroscopic data while it would miss some objects with low-level star formation (cite: 2017ApJ...841L...6B). 5 of 26 $UVJ$-selected QGs are detected in the PACS or MIPS band. It is not straightforward to estimate SFRs of QGs from the IR emission because the IR-based SFRs may be overestimated by contributions from evolved stellar populations (cite: 2014ApJ...783L..30U; 2019ApJ...877..140L) or time-averaging effects for recently quenched galaxies (cite: 2014MNRAS.445.1598H). The 5 QGs with IR detection are located near the bottom of the main sequence even if the IR emission is all originating from massive young stars. They are not included in our sample but it is going to have a minimal impact on our statistical analysis of a representative star-forming population.

## Optical structure

Deep ${\it HST}$/WFC3 imagining data is available for our sample in the 3D-HST/CANDELS fields. Fitting of elliptical S$\acute{\mathrm{e}}$rsic models to the two-dimensional light profiles in the F160W-band image gives the structural parameters of the rest-frame optical emission: $R_\mathrm{e,opt}$, $n_\mathrm{opt}$, minor-to-major axis ratio $q_\mathrm{opt}$, and position angle $PA_\mathrm{opt}$ (cite: 2012ApJS..203...24V; 2014ApJ...788...28V; 2014ApJ...788...11L). We adopt the effective radius along the semi-major axis to avoid inclination and projection effects, except for Section [5](#sec;discussion) where the circularized effective radius is used. We do not use 6 objects (U4-4706, U4-7472, U4-16795, U4-23044, GS4-2467 and GS4-5217) for optical size arguments because the best-fit S$\acute{\mathrm{e}}$rsic index reaches the constrained limit ($n = 0.2$ or $n = 8.0$) or the effective radius is unreasonably large with $R_\mathrm{e,opt}>1$$''$ ($\sim10$ kpc).

![](image_Figure2.eps)

## ALMA observations

We have carried out ALMA observations of dust continuum emission in the mass-selected sample of SFGs at $z=2$. We use the band 7 receivers with the 64-input correlator in Time Division Mode in a central frequency of 345 GHz ($\sim$870 $\mu$m). The frequency range available does not cover intermediate-$J$ ($J_\mathrm{up}<7$) CO lines or atomic carbon lines at $z=2$. We sample a wide range of spatial frequency in the $uv$ plane by using two array configurations: compact array with baseline lengths of 15–300 m and extended array with 15–1260 m (Figure [2](#fig;uvcoverage)). The extended array data determine the spatial resolution of interferometric images produced through Fourier Transforms while the compact array data are crucial for measuring total fluxes, corresponding to visibility amplitudes in a zero baseline. If short baseline data were not sufficiently sensitive, the size measurements of 870 $\mu$m emission would be strongly biased by compact components in galaxies. The maximum recoverable scale of our ALMA observations is 6.7$''$, corresponding to $\sim$55 kpc at $z=2$. We performed new observations of 84 galaxies with the compact array in May-June 2018 and 66 galaxies with the extended array in September 2018. The typical on-source time with 43–48 antennas is 4–5 minutes with the compact array and 7–9 minutes with the extended array. For the other galaxies in our sample, we use ALMA archival data (2012.1.00245.S, 2012.1.00983.S, 2013.1.00205.S, 2013.1.00566.S, 2013.1.00884.S, 2015.1.00242.S, 2016.1.01079.S) to avoid duplicate observations. We utilize the Common Astronomy Software Application package (`CASA`; (cite: 2007ASPC..376..127M)) for the data calibration.

We create high-, intermediate-, and low-resolution images by changing the weights of visibilities. We clean images down to the 1.5$\sigma$ level in a circular mask with a diameter of 2$''$ (4$''$ only for low-resolution images) using the `CASA/tclean` task. First, we create high-resolution images by using the compact array data with $uv$-distance of $>180$ k$\lambda$ and all the extended array data and adopting a briggs weighting with a `robust` parameter of +0.5. The spatial resolution and the noise level is 0.2$''$–0.3$''$ ($\sim$2 kpc) and 60$\pm$7 $\mu$Jy, respectively. The high-resolution images are used only for visually inspecting the location and the morphology of the dust emission. Next, we create intermediate-resolution images by using all the compact array data and the extended array data with $uv$-distance of $<180$ k$\lambda$ and adopting `robust`=+2.0. The spatial resolution and the noise level is 0.8$''$–1.0$''$ ($\sim$7 kpc) and 61$\pm$6 $\mu$Jy, respectively. The intermediate-resolution images are useful for defining the signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) of 870 $\mu$m continuum emission while they are not sufficient for measuring the total fluxes from the whole galaxies. We therefore create low-resolution images from all the combined data with `uvtaper` = 4$''$ and `robust`=2.0, resulting in the noise level of 174$\pm$29 $\mu$Jy. The spatial resolution is 3.3$''$–3.5$''$ ($\sim$ 28 kpc), which should cover whole galaxies at $z=2$. Note that we do not primarily use these ALMA images for measuring the effective radius of 870 $\mu$m emission (section [4.1](#sec;vis-fitting)).

![](image_Figure3.eps)

# Results

## Detections of 870 $\mu$m continuum emission

We detect the 870 $\mu$m continuum emission from 74 of 85 galaxies at S/N$>5$, 62 of which have S/N$>10$, in the intermediate-resolution images. For 74 detected objects, we measure the total 870 $\mu$m flux density from the low-resolution images. As U4-7472 and U4-36568 have a companion 870 $\mu$m source within a radius of 1.5$''$, we create low-resolution images after subtracting the companion in the visibility plane to measure the flux densities (section [4.1](#sec;vis-fitting)). The median flux density is $S_\mathrm{image}=$1.8 mJy in the range from 0.4 mJy to 6.9 mJy. Dust continuum emission on the Rayleigh–Jeans regime is commonly used as a tracer of gas mass (cite: 2015ApJ...800...20G; 2016ApJ...820...83S; 2018ApJ...853..179T). We estimate gas mass in massive SFGs from the 870 $\mu$m flux density by using the calibration of (cite: 2016ApJ...820...83S). There is a clear trend of increasing flux density in the plane of stellar mass and offset of a galaxy from the star formation main sequence, SFR/SFR$_\mathrm{MS}$, defined by a broken power law model in (cite: 2014ApJ...795..104W). More massive, more actively star-forming galaxies are brighter at 870 $\mu$m (Figure [3](#fig;870flux)). From a linear fitting in this parameter space, we derive equations to predict a 870 $\mu$m flux density and a gas mass of SFGs as,

$$\begin{eqnarray}
\log S_\mathrm{870,fit} [\mathrm{mJy}]&=&(0.95\pm0.15) \log M_\star \nonumber\\
&&+ (0.52\pm0.08) \log (\frac{\mathrm{SFR}}{\mathrm{SFR}_\mathrm{MS}}) \nonumber\\
&& - (10.41\pm1.7), \label{eq:flux} \\
\log M_\mathrm{gas,fit} [M_\ensuremath{\odot}]&=&(0.95\pm0.15) \log M_\star \nonumber \\
&&+ (0.53\pm0.08)\log (\frac{\mathrm{SFR}}{\mathrm{SFR}_\mathrm{MS}}) \nonumber \\
&& + (0.33\pm1.7). \label{eq:Mgas}
\end{eqnarray}$$

![](image_Figure4.eps)

The dependence on SFR offset is identical to the general scaling relation covering the wide range of galaxy properties (cite: 2018ApJ...853..179T) while the mass-dependence is slightly stronger than in the scaling relation (exponent 0.67; (cite: 2018ApJ...853..179T)). The median and the standard deviation of the difference between the actual measurements and the best-fit values is $\log (S_\mathrm{image}/S_\mathrm{870,fit})=-0.03\pm$0.20 dex. On the other hand, there is a systematic error in the predictions by Equation ([\[eq:flux\]](#eq:flux)): the flux densities are overestimated at $S_\mathrm{image}<$1 mJy and underestimated at $S_\mathrm{image}>$3 mJy (Figure [4](#fig;870flux_fit)). It is possible to correct for the systematics by applying $S_\mathrm{870,fit,cor}=$1.86$S_\mathrm{870,fit}$-0.27, but the standard deviation of $\log (S_\mathrm{image}/S_\mathrm{870,fit,cor})$ increases to 0.27 dex. We also note that this prediction is valid only in the stellar mass range of $\log(M_\star/M_\ensuremath{\odot})>11$ and in the redshift range of $z=1.9-2.6$.

In addition to the primary targets of massive SFGs at $z\sim2$, we serendipitously detect 19 dust continuum sources at S/N$>$5.0 in the regions within 13.6 arcsec of the phase center, where the primary beam correction factor is less than 0.15 (Table [\[serendipitous_sourcelist\]](#serendipitous_sourcelist)). The median redshift is $z=2.7$ and the 870 $\mu$ m flux density ranges from 0.4 mJy to 6.8 mJy after the primary beam correction. One source (U4-36568b) does not have an optical counterpart and is likely to be a massive SFG at $z>3$ (cite: 2019Natur.572..211W). 4 of 19 have a similar redshift to the primary targets with $|\Delta z|<0.1$, suggesting that they are physically associated. In fact, one (GS4-44920 and GS4-45068) of the four pairs has been spectroscopically identified at $z=2.448-2.450$ (cite: 2013A&A...549A..63K), with a projected separation of 4$''$ ($\sim32$ kpc).

## Non-detected objects

For 11 non-detected objects, we give the 5$\sigma$ upper limit of the 870 $\mu$m flux density from the low-resolution images. 6 of them are very close to the boundary of the quiescent regime in the $UVJ$ diagram (cite: 2015ApJ...813...23V) and have the lowest SFRs in our sample. Given that they lie about 2 dex below the main sequence at $z\sim2$ in the $M_\star$–SFR diagram (Figure [1](#fig;UVJ)), they are no longer representative of the star-forming population. Therefore, we use the modified $UVJ$ criteria to define a clean sample of massive SFGs at $z\sim2$ as,

$$\begin{eqnarray}
V-J &<& 1.5, \nonumber \\
U-V &>& 1.3, \nonumber \\
U-V &>& 1.4(V-J)-0.1. \label{eq:UVJ}
\end{eqnarray}$$

The detection rate in the updated SFG sample increases from 87% to 94%, indicating it represents an almost mass-complete sample of SFGs down to $\log(M_\star/M_\ensuremath{\odot})=11$.

For one galaxy (GS4-40185) classified as QGs in the modified criterion, we detect the 870 $\mu$m continuum emission at S/N=5.5. This galaxy is located below the main-sequence with $\log$(SFR/SFR$_\mathrm{MS})=-0.76$. The gas mass fraction is $M_\mathrm{gas}/(M_\star+M_\mathrm{gas})$=15%. This is more than twice smaller than the median value (37%) in 78 SFGs including 5 non-detected sources and is comparable to the gas fraction of a post-starburst galaxy at $z=0.7$ (cite: 2017ApJ...846L..14S). The less active star formation and the small gas fraction suggest that star formation is being quenched. Given that other 6 galaxies with similar quiescent $UVJ$ colors are not detected at 870 $\mu$m, GS4-40185 is a good candidate for studying the quenching mechanism, that probably works on a short timescale.
